_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: A calamity awaits him: [this refers] to one over whom forty days have passed without suffering.
rashi:a2.1: Before the rebuke: for He would reprove them for their deeds.
rashi:a3.1: What is that which is written: “This is the generation of them that seek after Him [dorshav]”: it juxtaposes the generation [dor] to those who seek after Him [dorshav, i.e., its leaders].
rashi:a4.1: For good: with regard to piety.
rashi:a5.1: What is different that “in the beginning [bereshit]” is written with regard to Jehoiakim and Zedekiah? Because the Holy One, Blessed be He, sought to overturn the act of Creation [ma’aseh bereshit] in their days.
rashi:a9.1: Mishna. Affordability in accordance with the one taking the vow: the law of affordability, that a poor person is judged in valuations according to his means, as it is written: “But if he is too poor for your valuation” (Leviticus 27:8). We follow the one taking the vow and not the subject of the vow, as is explained below.
rashi:a9.2: And the years in accordance with the subject of the vow: as is explained below, a young person who valuated an elderly person gives the valuation of an elderly person. For we do not follow the years of the one taking the vow himself, since he did not say: My valuation is upon me, but rather: The valuation of so-and-so is upon me. And the valuation of an elderly person, from sixty years and up, is less than the valuation of a young person.
rashi:a9.3: And the valuations in accordance with the one valuated: the fixed sum of the valuation for a male and a female follows the one valuated and not the one who valuates, as is explained below: a man who valuated a woman, saying: The valuation of so-and-so [a woman] is upon me, gives the valuation of the one valuated.
rashi:a9.4: At the time of the valuation: as is explained below, that if he valuated himself when he was less than twenty years old, which is the valuation of a minor, and before he gave it he became twenty, he gives only according to the time when he first valuated.
rashi:a12.1: I say: even with regard to valuations it is so: if a case should occur with valuations similar to the offerings, it would be like the offerings. As for what you said, that valuations are not like offerings, that is because the cases are not similar to one another. For why does a poor person who valuated a wealthy person give the valuation of a poor person, according to his means? Because the wealthy person is not obligated anything, and it is not similar to the leper [who is himself obligated in his offering]. And this one who spoke of the wealthy person intended only the measure of the wealthy person’s years, which are fewer or more than his own years. Therefore he is judged by affordability, for he specified nothing except that he took upon himself the valuation of the measure [of the years] of the wealthy person, and the law of a valuation is that it is judged by affordability.
rashi:a12.2: But a wealthy person who said: My valuation is upon me: who is obligated in a full valuation, similar to a wealthy leper; and a poor person heard, etc.
rashi:a13.1: Gemara. And he objects: Affordability applies to one who valuates: and not to one who vows. For one who says: My worth is upon me, is not judged by affordability; rather, he gives all of it when he is able, as we say in the chapter HaOmer Mishkali Alai (below, Arakhin 20a): Vows are more stringent than valuations, in that vows are not judged by affordability.
rashi:a13.2: And he answers: As it is written: “According to the means,” etc.: that is to say, the reason he calls the one who valuates “one who vows” here is that he adopted the wording of the verse.
rashi:a14.1: The years in accordance with the one valuated and not the subject of the vow: for one who says: The worth of so-and-so is upon me, is not judged according to the measure of years, but according to what that so-and-so would sell for in the market.
rashi:a16.1: And even though the one who vows for him is wealthy?: this is a question [i.e., can that be so?]. “The one who vows for him [madiro]” is the one who said: The offering of the leper is upon me.
rashi:a17.1: Perhaps on him: on the leper the Merciful One had compassion in his poverty, but not on the one who vows for him, even though he is poor.
rashi:a20.1: What is: But with regard to offerings that is not so?: But with offerings too you follow the one taking the vow!
tosafot:a9.1: Mishna. Affordability in accordance with the one taking the vow, and the years in accordance with the subject of the vow, and the valuations in accordance with the one valuated: This is puzzling: why did he not combine them together and teach: The years and the valuations are in accordance with the one valuated? And it is further puzzling: why did he not teach: A male gives the valuation of a female [i.e., state the case directly], and then it would not have been necessary below to say: The valuations in accordance with the one valuated, etc.?
tosafot:a10.1: How so? A poor person who valuated a wealthy person, etc.: [this was explained] above (Arakhin 7b), in the chapter Ein Ne’erakhin Paḥot, etc. [The printed text has the words “Rashi explained” in parentheses here.]
tosafot:a13.1: Affordability in accordance with the one taking the vow? It applies to one who valuates: that is, specifically to one who valuates and not to one who vows, as we say below in the chapter HaOmer Mishkali (Arakhin 20a): Vows are more stringent than valuations, in that vows take effect on an animal and a bird, and they are not judged by affordability, which is not so with valuations. [The printed text adds in parentheses: And it comes to exclude a wealthy leper.]
tosafot:a15.1: Affordability in accordance with the one taking the vow; how so? A poor person who valuated a wealthy person gives the valuation of a poor person: from the mouth of Rabbi Menaḥem of Joigny: for example, a wealthy person who said: My valuation is upon me, and a poor person heard and said: This is upon me, gives the valuation of a poor person. But with offerings it is not so: if one said: The offering of this leper is upon me, etc. On this Rabbi disagrees and says: A wealthy person who said: My valuation is upon me, and a poor person heard and said: What this one said is upon me, gives the valuation of a wealthy person, as with offerings. And so the explanation of the mishna implies.
tosafot:a19.1: But if the one who vows for him is wealthy, so too he brings in wealth? If so, what is: But with regard to offerings it is not so?: For with offerings the law is the same: if a wealthy person said: The offerings of this poor leper are upon me, he brings a wealthy person’s offering. So what difference is there between offerings and valuations? And he answers: One [clause] is about a wealthy leper whose vower is poor. For with a leper, if a poor person said: The offering of this wealthy leper is upon me, he gives [that] of a wealthy person, since we do not follow the one who vows; whereas with valuations we follow the one who vows, for if a wealthy person said: My valuation is upon me, and a poor person heard [and said]: What this one said is upon me, he gives the valuation of a poor person, since we follow the one who vows. Therefore “he” is needed to exclude [the leper], that there we do not follow the one who vows as with valuations. But according to Rabbi, who says that valuations and the offering are equal in this law, “he” is not needed to exclude a wealthy leper whose vower is poor, who gives [the offering] of a wealthy person, since with valuations the law is the same. Rather, “he” is needed to exclude a poor leper whose vower is wealthy: it might enter your mind that since Rabbi follows the obligation of the person, here too we should follow the obligation of the person and bring a poor person’s offering; it teaches us that it is not so. But according to the Rabbis, “he” is not needed to exclude a poor leper whose vower is wealthy: since with valuations we follow the one who vows, it is obvious that with the leper too we follow the one who vows, and “he” is not needed for this, as I explained. And so Rashi explained, and when we analyze the discussion here, so it is. But Rabbi’s view requires study: he compares a wealthy person who said: My valuation is upon me, to the offerings of a wealthy leper, where a poor person who vows must bring a wealthy person’s offering; and that is specifically when the poor person said: The offerings of this leper are upon me, to exempt him. And if he said so with valuations, what is the reason of the Rabbis? Since he said: What this one said is upon me, to exempt him, he has then explicitly vowed fifty sela, so how is he exempted with a poor person’s valuation?
gershom:a1.1: A calamity awaits him: and if one of these [sufferings] befalls him within forty days, he is saved from that calamity.
gershom:a2.1: “The righteous acts of the Lord, which He did [to you and to your fathers]”: this teaches that He acted with your fathers in righteousness and not by strict judgment.
gershom:a3.1: “This is the generation of them that seek after Him”: that is to say, as the generation, so are those who seek after Him, namely, its leaders.
gershom:a4.1: With regard to harshness and gentleness: that is to say, if the leader is exacting, so is the whole community; and likewise, if he is humble, they are all so as well.
gershom:a5.1: We will return to you, Yesh BaArakhin. [Rabbeinu Gershom marks the end of the chapter here.]
gershom:a6.1: Affordability in accordance with the one taking the vow: affordability, as it is written: “According to the means of him who vowed shall he valuate him”: we follow the means of the one who valuates, that is, the one taking the vow, as is explained in the Gemara, and not the one valuated, as he explains: How so? A poor person who valuated, etc.
gershom:a7.1: And the years in accordance with the subject of the vow: that is, as the valuation written [in the Torah], whether from a month old or from twenty years: we follow the years of the one valuated and not of the one who valuates. And he explains: How so, etc., for each one.
gershom:a8.1: But with regard to offerings [that is not so]: for we do not follow the means of the one who vows for him but [of the subject of the vow], as he explains: If one said: The offerings of this leper are upon me. [A note in the printed text suggests reading: If this one in whose place he brings was a poor leper, etc.]
gershom:a9.1: If it was a poor leper, [he brings a poor person’s offering], etc.
gershom:a10.1: And he asks: Why does the tanna teach affordability in accordance with the one taking the vow? With vows we do not follow affordability, only with valuations, with the one who valuates. And he answers that this “one taking the vow” that he teaches is the one who valuates. And why does he teach “one taking the vow”? He follows the language of the verse, as it is written: “According to the means of him who vowed shall he valuate him.” [A note in the printed text gives the end as:] And since he calls the one who valuates “one who vows,” he also says: The years in accordance with the subject of the vow.
gershom:a11.1: The Merciful One made affordability depend on the one who vows: for if he is poor, he gives a sela and is exempt, even if he becomes wealthy afterward; and if he did not give the sela in his poverty, if he becomes wealthy he gives the full valuation.
gershom:a12.1: But with regard to offerings that is not so: rather, we make the affordability depend on the subject of the vow.
gershom:a13.1: And even though the one who vows for him is wealthy?: he brings a poor person’s offering when the subject of the vow is poor?
gershom:a14.1: But “if he is poor”: of the one bringing the offering the Merciful One said that he brings a poor person’s offering; and this one who vows for him is obligated to bring a wealthy person’s offering. So why does he bring a poor person’s offering?
gershom:a15.1: When the one who vows for him was [also] poor: therefore he brings a poor person’s offering.
gershom:a16.1: [And why?] Perhaps on him: on the leper himself, when he is poor, the Merciful One had compassion, that he may bring in poverty; but on the one who vows for him, who said: His offerings are upon me, even though he is poor, the Merciful One did not have compassion, and he must bring a wealthy person’s offering. For it is written “he,” that is to say, he, the leper, brings in poverty, but not the one who vows for him.
gershom:a17.1: [Rav Adda said: It is further written:] “And his means do not suffice”: this did not need to be written, since it is written: “And if he is poor.” Rather, “and his means do not suffice” comes to include the one who vows for him, that when he is poor he too brings a poor person’s offering.
gershom:a18.1: But if the one who vows for him is wealthy, [what?] So too [he brings in wealth], even though the leper is poor? Evidently we follow the one who vows for him. What then is: But with regard to offerings that is not so, that is to say, that we follow the subject of the vow? For we see from the precise reading that we [also] follow the one who vows for him, as with valuations.
gershom:b1.1: Actually, with offerings we follow the subject of the vow, that is, the leper; and one is about a poor leper, etc. For two exclusions are written in the verse. One, “and his means do not suffice,” comes for a poor leper whose vower is poor, that the vower brings in poverty, as we said: “and his means do not suffice” includes the one who vows. But from here we still do not learn “but with regard to offerings that is not so”; for since the vower too is poor, even though he brings in poverty, we do not know whether we follow the subject of the vow or the vower. Rather, from here we learn that with offerings it is not so: one, for it is written “and if he is poor,” he, the leper, brings in poverty, to exclude a wealthy leper whose vower is poor, that the vower does not bring in poverty but in wealth; [and from this we know that we follow the subject of the vow and not the vower]. And this is: But with regard to offerings that is not so; rather, we make the affordability depend on the subject of the vow, the leper. For it might enter your mind to say: since the vower was included for the offering of a poor leper from “and his means do not suffice” [to bring in poverty], he is now also included even though the leper is wealthy, since the vower is poor, that he [too] brings in poverty. It teaches us “he”: that we depend on the poverty of the leper, as it is taught: Since we find, etc. [The printed text has editorial corrections in this note; we follow them.]
gershom:b2.1: Might this too be so: one who said: The offering of this wealthy leper is upon me, and he is poor, that he should bring in poverty; the verse states: “If he is poor,” to exclude the vower.
gershom:b3.1: And according to Rabbi, who says [I say: even with regard to valuations it is so]: similar to one who said: [The offering of this leper] is upon me, where we follow the leper, so too Rabbi says regarding valuations: if [one] said: My valuation is upon me, and another heard and said: What this one valuated [for himself] is upon me, to give it for him, then if the one vowed about was wealthy, he must give the valuation of a wealthy person, even though the one who vows for him is poor. Evidently, according to Rabbi’s reasoning, in valuations too we follow the means of the subject of the vow.
gershom:b4.1: But a wealthy leper whose vower is poor does not need the verse “he” to exclude, for [from the mishna] we have learned that we follow the obligation of the person who is the subject of the vow.
gershom:b5.1: Rather, according to Rabbi, “he” excludes what?
gershom:b6.1: To exclude a poor leper whose vower is wealthy: that we follow his vower and he brings in wealth, for it is written “he”: on him the Merciful One had compassion, and not on his vower.
gershom:b7.1: For it might enter your mind to say: since Rabbi said we follow the obligation of the person, where the subject of the vow is obligated, for example a wealthy person who said: My valuation is upon me, where the subject of the vow is obligated, [we follow the subject of the vow].
gershom:b8.1: Here too: since the leper is obligated, let us follow him; and he is poor, so let his vower bring in poverty.
gershom:b9.1: It teaches us “he”: he brings in poverty, but if his vower is wealthy, he brings in wealth, for it is written: “According to the means of him who vowed,” and he can afford it.
gershom:b10.1: Mishna. Rabbi says: I say: even with regard to valuations it is so: as with offerings, where we follow the subject of the vow.
gershom:b11.1: For why, etc.: that is to say, [if so,] why does the first clause of the mishna teach: A poor person who valuated a wealthy person gives the valuation of a poor person, following the means of the one taking the vow? Because the wealthy person who is valuated is not obligated anything. But a wealthy person who said: [My valuation is upon me, who is obligated in his valuation, and a poor person heard], etc., we follow the means of the subject of the vow, similar to offerings.
gershom:b12.1: He was poor [when he valuated and did not manage to give until he became wealthy, or wealthy and became poor, he gives the valuation of a wealthy person]; and it is explained in the Gemara. [A note in the printed text suggests reading: and the Gemara explains the reason of the first tanna, and the reason of Rabbi Yehuda as well.]
gershom:b13.1: “That he can afford [asher tasig yad]”: implies that we follow the time of handing over [the payment, and not the time of the vow; and now he is wealthy].
gershom:b14.1: “According to [al pi] the means of him who vowed”: implies that we follow the mouth [peh], that is, the time of the vow.
gershom:b15.1: Until he is in his poverty [from his beginning until his end]: but if he became wealthy in between, he gives the valuation of a wealthy person.
gershom:b16.1: “And if he is poor”: which is written with regard to a leper.
gershom:b17.1: Who brought his offerings: one of his offerings when he was poor, and he became wealthy before he brought the others.
gershom:b18.1: Or he brought one when he was wealthy and became poor: everything follows the sin offering: for if he brought a bird sin offering in poverty, even though he became wealthy he also brings a bird burnt offering in poverty; or if he brought an animal sin offering in wealth, even though he became poor he brings an animal burnt offering.
gershom:b19.1: Everything follows the guilt offering: for if he brought his guilt offering in wealth, even though he became poor he brings everything in wealth; and if he brought the guilt offering when he was poor, even though he became wealthy, since he began to bring the guilt offering in his poverty, he brings the rest in poverty.
gershom:b20.1: And likewise, everything follows the two birds: if he brought them in his poverty, even though he afterward became wealthy, he brings the rest in poverty. Evidently we do not say: until he is in his poverty from his beginning until his end.
gershom:b21.1: Wasn’t it stated about this: that this is why they disagree in this, that they derived from one verse, etc.
gershom:b22.1: An item that atones: for sin, that is, the sin offering. For we said above: Leprous marks come on account of seven things, and the sin offering atones; that is his purification, and everything follows it.
gershom:b23.1: An item that renders him fit: for consecrated food, to return to eating it; that is, the guilt offering.
gershom:b24.1: That which causes him purity, and what is it? The birds: as it is written: “Then shall the priest command to take for him that is to be purified [two living clean birds]” (Leviticus 14:4).
gershom:b25.1: But since we do not expound [“if he is poor”] to mean: until he is in poverty from his beginning until his end,
gershom:b26.1: [Rather,] “he”: why do I need “if he is poor” with regard to a leper?
gershom:b27.1: According to Rabbi as he holds: as we said above: according to Rabbi, to exclude a poor leper whose vower is wealthy, and according to the Rabbis, to exclude a wealthy leper whose vower is poor.
gershom:b28.1: But if so, according to Rabbi Yehuda, who expounds “but if he is too poor”: until he is in his poverty, etc., so too, etc.
gershom:b29.1: “And he is a witness”: until he is fit.
rashi:b1.1: And he answers: One is about a poor leper whose vower is poor, and one is to exclude a wealthy leper whose vower is poor: that is to say, certainly one of these statements of the mishna, namely the one that teaches: If it was a poor leper he brings a poor person’s offering, certainly speaks where his vower is poor, as we established. And from the other statement we derive that with offerings it is not so, which teaches: If it was a wealthy leper he brings a wealthy person’s offering, even though his vower is poor; and this is to exclude the vower from the law of valuations, for [here] we do not follow the one who vows.
rashi:b2.1: It might enter your mind to say, etc.: that is to say, and it was necessary to teach us “but with regard to offerings that is not so,” to teach us that where the leper is wealthy and his vower poor, he brings a wealthy person’s offering. For it might enter your mind to say: since the one who vows was included from “and his means do not suffice,” in that the Merciful One had compassion on him when he is poor and the leper is poor, he is also included even where the leper is wealthy, since he is poor; it teaches us [otherwise]. To me it seems, and this is the main reading, that the text reads: If so, what is: But with regard to offerings that is not so? It is about one case, about a wealthy leper whose vower is poor; it might enter your mind, etc. But I learned it as it is written in the books, and its explanation is as I have explained it, though that is not the [natural] flow of the Talmud.
rashi:b3.1: Might this too be so: a poor person who said: The offering of this wealthy leper is upon me.
rashi:b3.2: “If he is poor”: the Merciful One had compassion on him, and not on the one who vows for him.
rashi:b4.1: And according to Rabbi, who says: Even with regard to valuations it is so: that if a wealthy person was obligated in a valuation and a poor person said: What this one said is upon me, he gives the valuation of a wealthy person. Evidently we follow the obligation of the person valuated, where he is obligated something, similar to the leper. And so a wealthy leper whose vower is poor needs no exclusion, for we derive from valuations that he brings in wealth.
rashi:b5.1: To exclude a poor leper whose vower is wealthy: that he brings in wealth. And according to the Rabbis it is not necessary to exclude this, for since in valuations we follow the one who vows, with the leper too we follow the one who vows. But according to Rabbi it is necessary for this.
rashi:b6.1: Mishna. He was poor and became wealthy: before giving, or wealthy and became poor before giving, he gives the valuation of a wealthy person.
rashi:b7.1: But with regard to offerings that is not so: for if the leper was wealthy and became poor, or poor and became wealthy, everything follows the bringing of his offerings, as is stated in the baraita in the Gemara: A leper who brought his offerings, etc. The reason is that it is fixed in the verse, for one Sage as he holds and for the other Sage as he holds; but from the words of all of them we learn that we follow the bringing of his offerings.
rashi:b7.2: Even if his father died, etc.: this refers to valuations, and it is a matter in its own right: even if the father of this one who valuates died at the time the priest valuates him and left him ten thousand maneh, or his ship, etc. And in the Gemara it is explained. [Rashi thus reads this clause as a separate ruling about valuations, where the Davidson English joins it to the leper’s offerings.]
rashi:b8.1: Gemara. Wealthy and became poor: “According to the means of him who vowed”: which implies that we follow the time of the vow.
rashi:b11.1: Who brought his offerings: some of his offerings.
rashi:b11.2: Everything follows the sin offering: if he brought an animal sin offering in wealth, he also brings an animal burnt offering; and if he brought a bird sin offering in poverty, even though he became wealthy he also brings a burnt offering in poverty.
rashi:b12.1: After the birds: the two live birds that he brings for the sprinkling before the shaving. If at the time they sprinkled on him he was poor, he brings his offerings in poverty; and if at that time he was wealthy, he brings all his offerings in wealth.
rashi:b13.1: They derived from one verse: for it is a Torah edict.
rashi:b13.2: An item that atones: for so it is written with regard to the poor leper: “And the priest shall atone for him” [Leviticus 14:31], and adjacent to it is this verse: “This is the law of him in whom is the mark of leprosy,” etc., which implies: one whose means do not suffice at the time of atonement shall have this law of poverty, even though his means suffice afterward.
rashi:b14.1: An item that renders fit: for so it implies: one whose means do not suffice at the time of his purification shall have the law of poverty. And the purification is the guilt offering, which renders him fit to enter the Temple and to eat consecrated food, for he places from the blood of the guilt offering on the thumbs and on the ridge of the ears.
rashi:b14.2: The birds cause him purity: for as long as he does not bring the birds, he cannot shave.
rashi:b15.1: According to Rabbi as he holds, etc.: as we expounded above.
rashi:b17.1: A blind person is unfit for testimony: for we require “or he has seen.”
tosafot:b3.1: Since we find with regard to valuations: This is puzzling: even without this reason of “we find with regard to valuations,” it should have said with regard to a leper that a poor person who said: The offering of the leper is upon me, gives [the offering] of a poor person, from the inclusion of “and his means do not suffice,” to include the one who vows, as was expounded above. And one can say: In any case, had we not found such a case with valuations, we would not have expounded [the case of] a poor person who valuated a wealthy person from the inclusion of the verse “and his means do not suffice.”
tosafot:b5.1: Here too we follow the obligation of the person; it teaches us [otherwise]: Rabbeinu Elḥanan asked: Since we say according to Rabbi that with a poor leper whose vower is wealthy we would follow the obligation of the person were it not for the exclusion of the verse, then with valuations too let us say so: that if a poor person said: My valuation is upon me, and a wealthy person heard and said: What this one said is upon me, he gives the valuation of a poor person, since we have no verse there to exclude [it and teach] that we do not follow the obligation of the person. And Rabbeinu Elḥanan answered: The leper is different, for there we would say that we follow the obligation of the person were it not for the verse that excludes it, since he vows only the leper’s offering specifically. But with valuations, where the wealthy person said: What this poor person said is upon me, it is obvious that we do [not] follow the obligation of the person: for even if the poor person were obligated nothing, and the wealthy person said: The valuation of so-and-so is upon me, he would give the valuation of a wealthy person; all the more so when [the poor person] was obligated, we have no reason to reduce the wealthy person to giving a poor person’s valuation.
tosafot:b7.1: But with regard to offerings [etc.], even if his father died: One cannot explain [this to mean] that with valuations, if the priest valuated him when he was poor, he waits until his father, who was wealthy, dies, and then gives the valuation of a wealthy person. For it says in the Tosefta of Arakhin: A poor person who valuated himself, we do not tell him: Do work and bring the valuation of a wealthy person; rather, it is better that he bring the valuation of a poor person than bring the valuation of a wealthy person after some time. Evidently, we do not wait. Rather, this is its explanation: even if his father died who was dying, as the Gemara [on 18a] establishes it: with the leper’s offering, if his father was dying at the time he brought the sin offering, and before he managed to bring [the rest of] his offerings his father died, the Temple has no share in them. [But with valuations it is not so]: since the priest did not valuate him as poor, to give a sela, and before he finished giving the sela his father died, and he became wealthy, he gives the valuation of a wealthy person. But it is difficult: why does the Gemara object: It is obvious? It comes to teach us a great deal: that if his father died before he managed to bring his offerings and he became wealthy, the Temple has no share in them! And one can say that it refers to the statement of Rabbi Yehuda, who said: Poor and became wealthy and again became poor, he gives the valuation of a wealthy person. But with offerings, [even if] his father died, for example, he was dying, as the Gemara establishes it, for example, he was initially wealthy and became poor, and now he is close to becoming wealthy from his father’s inheritance, even so the Temple has no share in them. And the Gemara objects: It is obvious that the Temple has no share in them, since he never had that money.
tosafot:b14.1: Rabbi Yehuda holds: the item that renders him fit, and what is it? The guilt offering: And if you say: But it says below in the chapter HaOmer Mishkali Alai (Arakhin 21a) (and in the third chapter of Nazir, 19a): Just as his sin offering and his guilt offering are indispensable, so his burnt offering is indispensable. [So] the sin offering and the burnt offering [are also indispensable], yet only the guilt offering is called what renders fit? And one can say: Certainly all of them are indispensable for eating consecrated food; for the sin offering, atonement applies to it more than to the guilt offering, since the guilt offering’s whole essence is only to render the leper fit, for he places [blood] from the guilt offering on him, [on] the thumbs. Therefore he calls it the item that renders him fit.
tosafot:b17.1: Before he became his son-in-law, and he became his son-in-law, and afterward his daughter died, he is fit: this speaks where his daughter has no children, since we establish it here in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds (Sanhedrin 27b): If he was his son-in-law and his daughter died, if she has children from him, he is a relative; but if he has no children, he is not a relative.
